name: Stair and Landing Core
description: The vertical circulation treated as a room rather than a device. Where a stair is a room you arrive in, the upper floor gets a privacy buffer and the house gets its best window; where it is a fire escape in a slot, both are lost.

rooms.note: Under the stair, and the only genuinely free storage in a house.

internal_rules.statement: A window on the half-pace or at the head. A stair lit only from the floors it connects is a shaft.
Landing depth not less than the stair width. Below that it is a turn, not a landing.
No bedroom door opens directly onto a landing visible from the hall below.
Riser and tread constant through the whole flight, including at landings. A single odd riser is the most common cause of a domestic fall.
Where a back stair exists it lands in the service zone, never on the formal landing.

attaches_to.position: in the passage or a hall off it
steep and winding beside the central stack, which is the type's known compromise

attaches_to.note: Single storey; where a ranch has a stair it is to a cellar and belongs in the service core.

expansion_logic: Widen rather than lengthen. A stair hall gains far more from an extra two feet of width than from a longer run.
servicing_strategy: The stack of the house: an opening landing window is the cheapest summer ventilation available, and the stair is the path the air takes.

style_variation.note: The half-pace window is frequently the most elaborate on the house.
Open stringer, landing seat, and the stair often visible from the living room as a piece of joinery.
Stair in the narrow dimension, lit from the piazza side.

sources: Waterman, The Dwellings of Colonial America
